screens.title: Libraries and Advanced Data Structures
screens.narratorSegment: In this chapter you'll learn how Solidity libraries and advanced data structures let you organize contract code and state for clarity, safety, and gas efficiency. Libraries let you factor common utilities into shared code that executes in the calling contract's context, reducing deployment repetition and improving maintainability. You'll also learn how to attach library functions to concrete types with the using for directive, and how to model real-world entities with structs, enums, nested mappings, and dynamic arrays. We will show practical patterns such as storing structs inside mappings, iterating with care, and avoiding costly on-chain loops. A concrete hands-on example in this chapter builds an ArrayUtils library and a Marketplace contract that uses nested mappings and an array of IDs to manage products. You will see how removing an ID from a seller's list can be delegated to a reusable library to avoid duplication and to keep the main contract focused on business rules. Finally, we'll discuss storage versus memory behavior and storage slot packing so you understand how ordering fields affects gas. By the end you will be able to choose the right structure for common design patterns and implement small libraries to keep code modular. What is one small utility you could extract from a contract you wrote recently?

Module 3›Chapter 3.3›Libraries & Data Structures
Libraries and Advanced Data Structures
Reusable helpers, typed extensions, nested mappings, and efficient collections for Solidity.
In this lesson

Understand why libraries exist, how using for binds helpers to types, and how to design structs, enums, nested mappings and arrays safely.

Coming up

A hands-on ArrayUtils and Marketplace example will show array removal, nested mappings, and practical gas considerations.

Why this matters

Modular libraries and well-chosen data structures reduce bugs, improve reuse, and let you reason about gas costs when designing real contracts.

Concept map
Libraries, using for, structs, mappings, arrays, packing
Library
Stateless helper functions and reusable logic.
Data Structures
Structs, enums, nested mappings, arrays.
Using for
Attach helpers as methods on a type for readable calls.
Gas
Slot packing and avoiding large storage loops.
Explore Key Topics
Array utilities, nested mappings for ownership, storage packing strategies.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: These objectives guide our focus: we start by explaining why libraries exist and how they help with reuse and deployment costs. Then you'll learn how the using for directive attaches library functions to types so you can write clearer, method-style calls. Next we'll explore advanced struct and enum patterns, including nested mappings and arrays of structs that model complex state. Each objective includes a short skill you should be able to demonstrate by the end. For example, after practicing, you should be able to implement a small ArrayUtils library and use it inside a Marketplace contract to add and remove product IDs safely. You will also be able to explain storage versus memory semantics when you retrieve a struct from a mapping and why slot packing matters for gas. These goals are chosen so you can reason about both code organization and on-chain cost trade-offs. As you work through code examples, watch for common mistakes such as assuming a memory copy will persist to storage, or trying to use using for with unsupported external library functions.

First, you will implement the ArrayUtils library functions for removing elements and checking containment, and you will attach those functions with using for to uint256 arrays. screens.title: What is a Solidity library?
screens.narratorSegment: A Solidity library is a special source artifact designed to host reusable functions that operate on provided data rather than owning state. Libraries are stateless by default and cannot hold Ether. The key runtime difference is that public or external library functions are executed with a delegate-style call into the library code, so the library runs in the context of the calling contract. That means the storage layout used will be that of the calling contract, not the library. Internal library functions are inlined into the calling contract at compile time, resulting in function bodies embedded directly into bytecode. A concrete example is a Math library with an add helper: you can place that implementation in a library and then call it from many contracts. A common misconception is assuming libraries always reduce runtime gas; internal functions get inlined and may duplicate bytecode across contracts, while deployed libraries used via delegate calls avoid duplicated deployment costs but add an external call overhead. Key takeaway: libraries are a design tool for reuse and modularity, and you should choose internal versus public functions based on whether you want inlining or a shared deployed body. To practice, identify a small helper in your codebase and move it into a library to observe deployment and call differences.

content.html:
Module 3›Chapter 3.3›What is a Solidity library?
Definition
A library holds reusable functions that operate on data passed in, is stateless, and cannot hold Ether. It avoids repeating utility code across contracts.
Internal vs Public
Internal functions are inlined into contract bytecode. Public functions can be called via delegate-style calls that execute in caller storage context.
Common misconception
Assuming libraries always reduce runtime gas. Inlining may duplicate code; deployed libraries save deployment cost but use external call overhead.
Concrete example
A Math library with add, sub helpers that many contracts reuse. Deploy once for shared behavior, or inline for simple private helpers.
Illustration
library Math { function add(uint a, uint b) internal pure returns (uint) { return a + b; } }
Key Takeaway

Pick internal for simple inline helpers and public/external for a shared deployed library when you want one address to serve many contracts.

Check your understanding
Why might you choose a deployed library instead of inlining a helper? Think about deployment size and runtime call overhead.

screens.title: Internal vs Public library functions
screens.narratorSegment: Understanding the distinction between internal and public (or external) library functions is essential for designing both the runtime cost profile and the code organization of your contracts. Internal library functions are compiled into and inlined within the calling contract's bytecode. That means you pay the deployment cost per contract that includes the inlined code, but calls to those functions are direct and avoid delegate-call overhead. Public library functions, on the other hand, live at a deployed library address; calls to them from a contract typically use a delegate-style call that executes the library code in the caller's storage context. This allows a single deployed library to serve many contracts without duplicating its bytecode, saving total deployed size across a system. A common error is assuming the storage context is the library's; because delegate-style calls run in the caller's context, storage reads and writes impact the calling contract. Pick internal for tiny helpers you want optimized as direct calls and when code duplication is acceptable. Pick public or external library functions if you want to centralize logic at one address and avoid duplicating code across many deployments. Finally, remember delegate calls introduce a slight runtime cost for the call itself and require careful attention to storage layout compatibility.

content.html:
Module 3›Chapter 3.3›Internal vs Public
Internal functions
Inlined into bytecode. Direct calls, no delegate overhead. Larger bytecode per contract.
When to use
Small helpers where duplication is acceptable and you want minimal runtime call overhead.
Public / External functions
Deployed once, called via delegate-style calls. Saves deployment repetition but adds call overhead and storage-context considerations.
Visual comparison
Deployed size
Internal: larger per contract. External: single deployed library.
Call cost
Internal: direct. External: delegate call overhead.
Misconception
Don't assume a library has separate storage; delegate-executed functions act on the caller's storage layout.

screens.title: Using the using for directive
screens.narratorSegment: The using for directive lets you bind library functions to a specific type so those functions can be called in method-call style on variables. Conceptually this reads like attaching helper methods to a built-in or custom type. For example, if you have a library with functions that take a uint as the first argument, declaring using Math for uint; makes those functions available as uint methods. This improves readability and keeps call sites concise, especially for frequently used utilities or for operations on custom structs. Importantly, using for works with internal or public library functions but does not support external-only functions called via a library address. A practical example is attaching ArrayUtils to uint256[] so you can call productIds. remove(index) or productIds. contains(value). When you use using for on a struct type, methods can accept the struct as the receiver and encapsulate common mutations or validations. Watch for a common error: when a method modifies a struct you must ensure it's operating on storage rather than a memory copy, otherwise changes won't persist. As a rule, design using for helpers to accept storage references when they need to mutate state, and prefer pure or view helpers for read-only operations. Try designing a small remove function that swaps the last element into the removed slot and then pops, keeping it safe for unordered arrays.

keyIdea.text: Bind helpers to types to enable method-like calls and keep code readable; ensure storage vs memory semantics match the helper's intent.

content.html:
Module 3›Chapter 3.3›Using for directive
Pattern
using ArrayUtils for uint256[]; attaches ArrayUtils functions as methods on uint256 arrays, enabling clearer calls like ids.remove(i).
Design note
Helpers that mutate state should accept storage references; read-only helpers can be pure or view.
Concrete example
Attach remove and contains to uint256[] to make sellerProductIds management concise and reusable across contracts.
Code panel
// attach helpers
using ArrayUtils for uint256[];

// call style
productIds.remove(index);
productIds.contains(id);
Pitfall
Using for won't work with library functions that are external-only; prefer internal or public signatures for attachment.
Key Takeaway
Use using for to make code expressive, but ensure helper signatures and storage behavior are correct before attaching.

screens.title: ArrayUtils library: remove and contains
screens.narratorSegment: A compact ArrayUtils library demonstrates how small, well-tested helpers simplify contract logic. The remove helper uses the swap-and-pop pattern: it moves the last array element into the index being removed, then calls pop to shrink the array. This approach avoids shifting all later elements and keeps gas cost constant relative to the array length, which is essential when order is not important. The contains helper iterates the array to check for a value; this is fine for short arrays, but it becomes expensive for large arrays so use it sparingly or keep mappings for constant-time checks. When writing remove, include a bounds check to avoid out-of-range errors. Attach these functions using using ArrayUtils for uint256[]; so calls read naturally in the contract. A common mistake is assuming swap-and-pop preserves order; call remove only when order is not required. Another pitfall is iterating unbounded arrays in transactions that change state — prefer off-chain reads or paginated views when a client needs to scan long lists. After creating the library, run tests that confirm the element was removed and that contains reflects the new state.

keyIdea.text: Swap-and-pop gives constant-time removal for unordered arrays; contains is linear and should be used cautiously for large arrays.

content.html:
Module 3›Chapter 3.3›ArrayUtils library
Remove helper
Swap the last entry into the deleted index and pop to shrink. Include bounds checks to guard against invalid indices.
// behavior: index check, swap with last, pop
Contains helper
Linear scan to find a value. Suitable for short arrays; consider mapping for large sets.
Example call
After attaching the library with using for, call productIds.remove(index) from Marketplace to update the seller's list.
Misconception
Swap-and-pop preserves element order. It does not; use it only when order is irrelevant or can be reconstructed off-chain.
Key Takeaway
Small, focused library helpers keep your contract logic readable and centralize array operations for reuse.

screens.title: Modeling Products: Structs and Nested Mappings
screens.narratorSegment: Modeling domain entities on-chain often uses structs stored inside mappings for direct lookup. In the Marketplace example a Product struct holds id, name, price, seller, and available flag. The sellerProducts mapping is nested: mapping(address => mapping(uint256 => Product)) which gives each seller a mapping from product ID to Product. This pattern is powerful because it provides constant-time access to a specific product using the seller's address and product ID without scanning arrays. When you create a new product, initialize the struct in storage to avoid unnecessary copying. For example, allocate a storage reference to sellerProducts[msg. sender][productId] and then set fields; this updates storage directly. A common developer mistake is reading the struct into memory, modifying that copy, and assuming those changes persist. If you must modify in-memory copies, reassign the modified struct back into the mapping, but the usual approach is to work with a storage reference. Another consideration is event emission: emit events on add and remove so off-chain indexers can build efficient product lists without expensive on-chain enumeration. This architecture balances efficient reads for single items with a separate index (like an array of product IDs) for list operations.

keyIdea.title: Mapping strategy
keyIdea.text: Nested mappings let you index complex relationships directly; prefer storage references when mutating structs in mappings.

content.html:
Module 3›Chapter 3.3›Structs & Nested Mappings
Pattern
Use mapping(address => mapping(uint256 => Product)) to give each seller direct access to their products by ID with constant-time lookup.
Mutating storage
Acquire a storage reference like Product storage p = sellerProducts[msg.sender][id]; then set fields to persist changes.
Event guidance
Emit ProductAdded and ProductRemoved events so off-chain indexers can avoid on-chain enumeration when building lists.
Concrete snippet
sellerProducts[msg.sender][productId].name = newName; // ensure this is storage reference mutation
Common mistake
Reading a struct into memory, changing it, and not writing it back will not alter stored state.
Key Takeaway
Nested mappings provide fast direct access to items; combine them with arrays or events for list operations.

screens.title: Dynamic arrays of structs
screens.narratorSegment: Dynamic arrays of structs are a natural way to store an ordered collection when index-based iteration or enumeration is required. For example, User[] public activeUsers; collects users in insertion order and lets you iterate client-side or with controlled on-chain loops. However, iterating large arrays on-chain can be very gas-intensive. This makes arrays suitable when lists are known to be small, when you implement pagination, or when on-chain iteration is rare and audited. Mappings, by contrast, provide constant-time lookup without ordering and typically require an auxiliary index or array to enumerate values. A common design uses a mapping for direct access and an array of keys to support enumeration, while keeping operations that change the array minimized or offloaded off-chain. When pushing a struct into an array, push(User(addr, name, score)) constructs the struct in memory and stores it. Be careful with storage references: retrieving an element from a storage array returns a storage reference, while returning array elements to memory for external calls copies data. Consider also gas costs of copying large structs between memory and storage. The pragmatic pattern is to keep mappings for frequent direct lookups and use arrays for occasional enumeration, augmented by events so off-chain systems can index entries cheaply.

keyIdea.title: Array vs Mapping
keyIdea.text: Arrays offer ordered enumeration; mappings give direct lookup. Combine them and use events to avoid expensive on-chain scans.

content.html:
Module 3›Chapter 3.3›Dynamic arrays of structs
When to use arrays
Use arrays for ordered lists and small collections. Remember that on-chain iteration is expensive and can exceed gas limits for large arrays.
Push pattern
activeUsers.push(User(msg.sender, "Bob", 100)); creates and stores the struct in the array.
Best practice
Emit events for new entries and use off-chain indexing for heavy enumeration.
Design pattern
Combine mapping for direct access and an array of keys for enumeration; prefer pagination and off-chain reads to looping on-chain.
Performance note
Avoid full-array loops in functions that run in transactions; they can be exploited or simply revert due to gas limits.
Key Takeaway
Choose arrays for order and mappings for direct reads; use events and off-chain processing for heavy enumeration.

screens.title: Storage vs Memory for structs
screens.narratorSegment: When you retrieve a struct from storage the way you assign it determines whether you get a storage reference or a memory copy, and this choice controls whether your modifications persist. For example, Product storage p = sellerProducts[msg. sender][id]; gives a storage pointer so changes to p fields immediately update contract storage. By contrast, Product memory p = sellerProducts[msg. sender][id]; copies the struct into memory; modifying p will not change storage unless you explicitly write it back. This distinction matters because developers sometimes assume any retrieved struct behaves like a reference. Another subtlety occurs when returning structs from public view functions: returning a struct yields a memory copy for the external call. For heavy structs, copying between storage and memory costs gas. Therefore, when you need to mutate a struct stored inside a mapping or an array, use a storage reference. When you only need to read fields or return data to a caller, a memory copy is acceptable. A common misconception is believing memory copies are cheaper; while reads may be cheaper, copying large structs still incurs gas and should be minimized. Practically, prefer storage references for mutation and memory allocations for one-time reads or returns.

content.html:
Module 3›Chapter 3.3›Storage vs Memory
Rule of thumb
Use a storage reference when you want mutations to persist. Use memory for transient read-only copies or returns.
Mutation example
Product storage p = sellerProducts[msg.sender][id]; p.price = 200; // persists
Common error
Declaring memory for a retrieved struct and expecting updates to persist will lead to subtle bugs.
Practical tip
Minimize copying of large structs to keep gas low; read only required fields when possible.
Key Takeaway
Mutate via storage references; use memory for safe, temporary work and returns.

screens.title: Storage slot packing
screens.narratorSegment: Storage slot packing groups sequentially declared state variables into 256-bit slots when their sizes allow it, reducing the number of storage slots used and thus lowering gas costs. Solidity packs variables declared consecutively if their combined sizes fit within a single 32-byte slot. For example, two uint128 variables and one uint16 declared in sequence can share a single slot, whereas a uint256 followed by a uint8 will generally use two slots. The practical implication is that ordering fields from smallest to largest or grouping similar-sized fields can reduce storage usage. This matters especially for often-written variables because each storage slot costs gas when written. When designing structs that will be stored in a mapping or array, think about field sizes and grouping to maximize packing. A common oversight is neglecting to consider the compiler's packing rules when adding new fields to a struct, which can unexpectedly inflate storage usage. As a mitigation, review storage layout after changes and reorder fields if necessary. Remember that packing only occurs for tightly sequential fields of compatible types, so explicit attention to layout yields measurable gas savings over many writes.

screens.title: ArrayUtils + Marketplace: addProduct flow
screens.narratorSegment: Adding a product in the Marketplace ties together a few moving parts: the global product ID counter, the nested sellerProducts mapping, the sellerProductIds array, and the ArrayUtils helpers. The flow begins by incrementing the global nextProductId counter to assign a unique product ID. Then acquire a storage reference to sellerProducts[msg. sender][productId] and set the fields such as id, name, price, seller, and available. Next, push the new productId onto sellerProductIds[msg. sender] to keep an enumerable index. Emit a ProductAdded event so off-chain systems can index this addition. This separation of concerns keeps the product record in the nested mapping for direct lookup and the per-seller array for enumeration. When you later remove a product, mark it unavailable in the mapping and use the ArrayUtils. remove helper to update the id array. The architecture avoids expensive global scans: direct lookups are O(1) via nested mapping, and enumeration uses the id array combined with events so off-chain indexers can recreate lists efficiently. Test both the storage state and the emitted events to ensure off-chain consumers will have accurate data. screens.title: Marketplace: removeProduct and safety checks
screens.narratorSegment: Removing a product requires careful checks and consistency between the nested mapping and the seller's id array. First, verify that the caller owns the product by checking sellerProducts[msg. sender][_productId]. seller == msg. sender and that the product is currently available. To avoid permanently deleting storage, a safe pattern is to mark the product's available flag false so historical references remain readable. Then remove the productId from sellerProductIds[msg. sender] using the library's remove method which performs index bounds checks and swap-and-pop. Always ensure you find the correct index in the id array before calling remove, and fail early with a clear revert message if not found. After updating storage and the id array, emit ProductRemoved so off-chain indexers can update their view. Testing should include attempts to remove a non-existent id and attempts from non-owner addresses to confirm the require statements revert as expected. This pattern keeps mappings consistent with enumeration arrays and provides clear events for clients. Remember that marking available false is cheaper and safer than clearing all struct fields and prevents accidental reuse of the id without an explicit re-add.

In this chapter you'll learn how Solidity libraries and advanced data structures let you organize contract code and state for clarity, safety, and gas efficiency. Libraries let you factor common utilities into shared code that executes in the calling contract's context, reducing deployment repetition and improving maintainability. You'll also learn how to attach library functions to concrete types with the using for directive, and how to model real-world entities with structs, enums, nested mappings, and dynamic arrays. We will show practical patterns such as storing structs inside mappings, iterating with care, and avoiding costly on-chain loops. A concrete hands-on example in this chapter builds an ArrayUtils library and a Marketplace contract that uses nested mappings and an array of IDs to manage products. You will see how removing an ID from a seller's list can be delegated to a reusable library to avoid duplication and to keep the main contract focused on business rules. Finally, we'll discuss storage versus memory behavior and storage slot packing so you understand how ordering fields affects gas. By the end you will be able to choose the right structure for common design patterns and implement small libraries to keep code modular. What is one small utility you could extract from a contract you wrote recently?

These objectives guide our focus: we start by explaining why libraries exist and how they help with reuse and deployment costs. Then you'll learn how the using for directive attaches library functions to types so you can write clearer, method-style calls. Next we'll explore advanced struct and enum patterns, including nested mappings and arrays of structs that model complex state. Each objective includes a short skill you should be able to demonstrate by the end. For example, after practicing, you should be able to implement a small ArrayUtils library and use it inside a Marketplace contract to add and remove product IDs safely. You will also be able to explain storage versus memory semantics when you retrieve a struct from a mapping and why slot packing matters for gas. These goals are chosen so you can reason about both code organization and on-chain cost trade-offs. As you work through code examples, watch for common mistakes such as assuming a memory copy will persist to storage, or trying to use using for with unsupported external library functions.

This second objectives slide focuses on practice and mental checks. First, you will implement the ArrayUtils library functions for removing elements and checking containment, and you will attach those functions with using for to uint256 arrays. Practically, this means writing a remove routine that swaps and pops to avoid shifting linear costs when order is not required. Second, you'll implement a Marketplace contract that uses nested mappings from seller addresses to product structs, and a per-seller dynamic array of product IDs. The exercise guides you to add and remove products from a seller while observing event emissions for state changes. Third, you'll practice retrieving and modifying structs in storage versus memory so you understand when changes persist. Finally, you'll apply slot packing by grouping integer sizes to lower gas consumption. Each practice item is chosen so you can reason about correctness and gas tradeoffs, and to build small reusable libraries that make contracts easier to audit and reuse in other projects.

A Solidity library is a special source artifact designed to host reusable functions that operate on provided data rather than owning state. Libraries are stateless by default and cannot hold Ether. The key runtime difference is that public or external library functions are executed with a delegate-style call into the library code, so the library runs in the context of the calling contract. That means the storage layout used will be that of the calling contract, not the library. Internal library functions are inlined into the calling contract at compile time, resulting in function bodies embedded directly into bytecode. A concrete example is a Math library with an add helper: you can place that implementation in a library and then call it from many contracts. A common misconception is assuming libraries always reduce runtime gas; internal functions get inlined and may duplicate bytecode across contracts, while deployed libraries used via delegate calls avoid duplicated deployment costs but add an external call overhead. Key takeaway: libraries are a design tool for reuse and modularity, and you should choose internal versus public functions based on whether you want inlining or a shared deployed body. To practice, identify a small helper in your codebase and move it into a library to observe deployment and call differences.

Understanding the distinction between internal and public (or external) library functions is essential for designing both the runtime cost profile and the code organization of your contracts. Internal library functions are compiled into and inlined within the calling contract's bytecode. That means you pay the deployment cost per contract that includes the inlined code, but calls to those functions are direct and avoid delegate-call overhead. Public library functions, on the other hand, live at a deployed library address; calls to them from a contract typically use a delegate-style call that executes the library code in the caller's storage context. This allows a single deployed library to serve many contracts without duplicating its bytecode, saving total deployed size across a system. A common error is assuming the storage context is the library's; because delegate-style calls run in the caller's context, storage reads and writes impact the calling contract. Pick internal for tiny helpers you want optimized as direct calls and when code duplication is acceptable. Pick public or external library functions if you want to centralize logic at one address and avoid duplicating code across many deployments. Finally, remember delegate calls introduce a slight runtime cost for the call itself and require careful attention to storage layout compatibility.

The using for directive lets you bind library functions to a specific type so those functions can be called in method-call style on variables. Conceptually this reads like attaching helper methods to a built-in or custom type. For example, if you have a library with functions that take a uint as the first argument, declaring using Math for uint; makes those functions available as uint methods. This improves readability and keeps call sites concise, especially for frequently used utilities or for operations on custom structs. Importantly, using for works with internal or public library functions but does not support external-only functions called via a library address. A practical example is attaching ArrayUtils to uint256[] so you can call productIds. remove(index) or productIds. contains(value). When you use using for on a struct type, methods can accept the struct as the receiver and encapsulate common mutations or validations. Watch for a common error: when a method modifies a struct you must ensure it's operating on storage rather than a memory copy, otherwise changes won't persist. As a rule, design using for helpers to accept storage references when they need to mutate state, and prefer pure or view helpers for read-only operations. Try designing a small remove function that swaps the last element into the removed slot and then pops, keeping it safe for unordered arrays.

A compact ArrayUtils library demonstrates how small, well-tested helpers simplify contract logic. The remove helper uses the swap-and-pop pattern: it moves the last array element into the index being removed, then calls pop to shrink the array. This approach avoids shifting all later elements and keeps gas cost constant relative to the array length, which is essential when order is not important. The contains helper iterates the array to check for a value; this is fine for short arrays, but it becomes expensive for large arrays so use it sparingly or keep mappings for constant-time checks. When writing remove, include a bounds check to avoid out-of-range errors. Attach these functions using using ArrayUtils for uint256[]; so calls read naturally in the contract. A common mistake is assuming swap-and-pop preserves order; call remove only when order is not required. Another pitfall is iterating unbounded arrays in transactions that change state — prefer off-chain reads or paginated views when a client needs to scan long lists. After creating the library, run tests that confirm the element was removed and that contains reflects the new state.

This pattern is powerful because it provides constant-time access to a specific product using the seller's address and product ID without scanning arrays. When you create a new product, initialize the struct in storage to avoid unnecessary copying. For example, allocate a storage reference to sellerProducts[msg. sender][productId] and then set fields; this updates storage directly. A common developer mistake is reading the struct into memory, modifying that copy, and assuming those changes persist. If you must modify in-memory copies, reassign the modified struct back into the mapping, but the usual approach is to work with a storage reference. Another consideration is event emission: emit events on add and remove so off-chain indexers can build efficient product lists without expensive on-chain enumeration. This architecture balances efficient reads for single items with a separate index (like an array of product IDs) for list operations.

Dynamic arrays of structs are a natural way to store an ordered collection when index-based iteration or enumeration is required. For example, User[] public activeUsers; collects users in insertion order and lets you iterate client-side or with controlled on-chain loops.
